To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

drizzle and cloud‐top entrainment are the primary physical features responsible for the differences between adiabatic, homogeneous, and observed cloud profiles, and that these features can induce biases of 5–20 g/m2 in LWP retrievs.
(1) drizzle‐induced variability in the cloud vertical profile can lead to significant bias in LWP retrieals and (2) the impact of cloud top entrainments is smaller but still nonnegligible.

(1) cloud top entrainment and drizzle are the two main physical processes that cause LWP retrieval biases, (2) the impact of these physical processes on LWP retrievability is dependent on cloud regime, and (3) the impact of drizzle on LWP retrievsability is more significant than that of cloud top entrained air.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the impact of cloud vertical profiles on LWP retrievability and quantifying the magnitude of the bias introduced.
understanding the sensitivity of passive optical retrievals of LWP to cloud vertical structure and how this sensitivity is impacted by cloud regime.
understanding the physical mechanisms that cause LWP retrieval bias, and the results are used to inform the design of passive optical retrieval algorithms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impact of vertical profile on MODIS‐like retrievals is significant, but not large enough to warrant a change to the current MODIS algorithm.
drizzle‐inhibited and cloud top entrained profiles have the largest impacts on LWP retrieval biases.
the impact of vertical profile assumptions is not negligible for LWP retrievals in the presence of drizzle and cloud entrainment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the vertical profile assumption for shallow marine boundary clouds is sensitive to cloud regime, and that the adiabat is a more appropriate assumption than the homogeneous assumption.
the vertical profile sensitivity for bispectral retrievals is similar to that of passive polarimetry, but the magnitude is larger by a factor of 3.
the impact on MODIS‐like LWP retrievals of the cloud vertical profile is significant, but it is possible to mitigate this impact through the use of a more complex vertical profile assumption.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of vertical profiles on LWP retrievs is not negligible and that this impact is sensitive to cloud regime.
the impact of vertical profile features on passive optical LWP retrieval is highly sensitive to the cloud regime and should be accounted for in retrievals.

the cloud vertical profile assumption is an important source of error in LWP retrieval, and that the impact of the vertical profile assumption is sensitive to cloud regime and cloud microphysical properties.
